Home Depot's Golden Horseshoe
An illustrated companion to Acquired · Fall 2026, Episode 2

The Golden Horse­shoe

Two retail executives got fired in 1978 with no savings. With a Wall Street banker and a merchant in a powder-blue leisure suit, they built what the Acquired hosts call the best-performing stock since its 1981 IPO. Here is that story, aisle by aisle, and the business lessons the hosts pull out along the way.

The $1,000 question

Apple went public in December 1980. Home Depot followed the next year. The episode opens with a dare: put $1,000 into each at its IPO, hold, and reinvest the dividends. The hardware store wins.

By the hosts’ count, Home Depot is the best total-return stock in the S&P 500 since it listed. That $1,000 is now worth roughly $17 million, about 25% a year for 45 years. The same $1,000 in an index fund would be around $170,000. Ben jokes that he is a Vanguard guy.

The company is huge in ways that are easy to miss. It operates only in North America, yet it is the world’s largest specialty retailer. Only general merchants like Walmart, Amazon and Costco sell more. It employs around 470,000 people, more than any bank, more than Starbucks, and more than any big tech company except Amazon.

01Aisle
one
1921 – 1975

Before the Depot

Lumber at one store, tools at another, pipe fittings at a third. Home improvement was a scavenger hunt.

After the war, America built suburbs. That meant millions of new houses that would eventually need new roofs, fences and bathrooms. But the stores that sold those things were regional, clubby and unsophisticated. You bought lumber at a lumberyard, tools at the hardware store, plumbing at the supply house and plants at the nursery. The weekend do-it-yourselfer, David notes, was not yet a real category.

The largest operator was Lowe’s of North Carolina. It grew out of a 1921 general store and ran small stores in strip malls, about $150 million in revenue in total.

Then came the 1970s: oil shocks, stagflation, interest rates in the teens. Suburban retail went quiet. In Los Angeles, a holding company called Daylin had assembled a grab bag of chains, including pharmacies, discounters, clothing and home furnishings. David compares it to an index fund of retail. Nearly all of it was struggling. Daylin floated minority stubs of its subsidiaries, just under 20% so it could keep consolidating them, and those stubs traded at a discount to an already discounted parent.

One subsidiary was doing well: a hardware chain called Handy Dan.

LessonAisle 01
01

A fragmented industry is waiting for a new format, not a bigger store

Home improvement wasn’t short of stores. It was short of a format that put the lumberyard, hardware store, plumbing house and nursery under one roof at low prices.

02Aisle
two
1972 – April 1978

The Firing

A retailer with no equity, a finance whiz, a banker who bought the stock, and a turnaround CEO nicknamed after a comic-book villain.

B
Bernie MarcusNewark-born pharmacist turned retailer. CEO of Handy Dan from 1972, with no equity.
A
Arthur BlankYounger Daylin finance whiz Bernie brought in as Handy Dan’s CFO.
K
Ken LangoneLong Island banker who took Ross Perot’s EDS public. Almost never sells.
S
Sandy SigoloffDaylin’s turnaround CEO after its 1975 bankruptcy, nicknamed “Ming the Merciless.”

Bernie Marcus grew up poor in Newark during the Depression, the son of Jewish immigrants. His memoir says he ran with a gang as a kid. He was the first in his family to go to college, at Rutgers, and wanted to become a psychiatrist but couldn’t afford medical school. He became a pharmacist, then ran a store-within-a-store concession, then worked at the discounter Two Guys, then became an executive at Daylin. In 1972 Daylin made him CEO of Handy Dan. He owned none of it.

He recruited Arthur Blank, a young finance whiz from inside Daylin, as CFO. Ben’s favorite detail is that none of the founders were contractors or toolmakers. They were retail and finance people. Together they made Handy Dan the best operator in the industry, in the middle of a recession. Daylin went bankrupt anyway in 1975 and brought in Sandy Sigoloff to slash and burn.

Then a banker showed up. Ken Langone had taken a Philadelphia hardware chain public. Its CEO told him the best operator in the business was Handy Dan. Ken looked it up in Moody’s manual: the stock was about $3, and earnings were about $1.50 a share. It was trading at two years of earnings. He decided something had to be wrong.

Nothing was. Ken flew to LA, had lunch with Bernie, and told him to mortgage his house and buy stock. Bernie said it was too risky. Ken bought nearly every public share he could find himself, ending with almost 20% of the company. The one block he couldn’t buy was 50,000 shares owned by a Redemptorist church congregation in Brooklyn. The priest asked whether Ken was Catholic and Italian, and then told him the church would hold.

Interactive · step through the haggling

Ken’s stake, by offer

Offer amounts as recounted in the episode from Built from Scratch. Ben and the book disagree on the exact opening bids. The $25.50 sale in early 1978 is the consistent figure.

Sigoloff didn’t like a big outside shareholder flying to store openings with his managers. He wanted Ken out. Bernie urged Ken to sell. Ken warned him that once he was gone, Bernie would be next. Bernie trusted Sigoloff and said he could handle it. David points out that this trust was both Bernie’s flaw and the source of the loyalty people later felt toward him.

Ken sold in early 1978 for $25.50 a share. About three months later, in April 1978, Sigoloff fired Bernie, Arthur and an audit manager named Ron Brill. His pretext was a labor-relations investigation into his own company.

Bernie was 48, with no savings, no equity, a family to support, and an investigation hanging over him. Ken had heard Bernie’s idea years earlier, at a Handy Dan opening in Houston: someone was going to build a much bigger, cheaper store and put Handy Dan out of business. At breakfast, Ken told him the firing was the opportunity of a lifetime.

You just got kicked in the ass with a golden horseshoe.Ken Langone to Bernie Marcus, April 1978
LessonAisle 02
02

The worst day can be the golden horseshoe

Inside Daylin, Bernie could never build his store or own a piece of it. Being fired set him free. Ken also saw a mispriced asset in a public manual and acted on it fast.

03Aisle
three
Spring 1978

The Napkin Math

Take a warehouse club, fill it with a hardware store’s breadth, and staff it with people who know how to install things.

Bernie had visited Sol Price in San Diego. At Price Club, customers shopped off pallets. There was no back room, and the club bought straight from manufacturers, acting as its own wholesaler. Bernie’s warning to Ken had been simple: someday someone would bring this model to hardware.

Over dinner, Sol asked Bernie whether he was actually talented and could build something of his own. If so, Sol said, he should stop worrying about Sigoloff and go build it.

The pitch to investors came down to a few numbers. The best Handy Dan store did about $3 million a year. The new warehouse stores could do $7–9 million. Each would be around 60,000 square feet, with about 25,000 products instead of Handy Dan’s 8,000. Prices would be lower, with a 30% gross margin against the industry’s roughly 45%.

Two choices separated the plan from Price Club. The first was selection: Price Club carried about 4,000 items, a curated assortment. A project shopper needs every part, every time. The second was expertise: nobody needs help buying toilet paper, but most people need help hanging blinds or laying a floor.

Interactive · compare the formats

Three stores, side by side

LessonAisle 03
03

Combine two proven models into a new category

Price Club’s warehouse economics plus a hardware store’s breadth and advice. Neither model alone would have worked. Customers can’t install a floor off a pallet, and a 45%-margin hardware store can’t be the cheapest place in town.

04Aisle
four
Summer 1978

The Cadillac

Ross Perot offered $2 million for 70% of the company. The deal died over a car.

Ken flew everyone to Dallas. Ross Perot, whose EDS he had taken public, agreed to put up $2 million for 70%. Then it fell apart. When Bernie left Handy Dan, he kept the company car, an older Cadillac. Perot’s people drove Chevrolets, and he told Bernie that kind of thing mattered. Underneath, the problem was bigger: Perot would have run the company as a division of his empire, and Bernie wanted it to be theirs.

Ken had a different idea. Instead of giving up 70%, he would offer investors 50% for the same $2 million. Arthur asked how walking away from Perot could get them a better deal. Ken explained that retailers mark prices down when goods don’t sell, and in his business you mark them up. He then lined up about 40 individuals at roughly $50,000 apiece.

Who owns the company

Perot’s term sheet vs. Ken’s

~$223BRough value of Perot’s 70% today, per the hosts

The hosts’ estimate: 70% of a ~$350B company, adjusted for decades of dilution and buybacks (holders would keep roughly 91% or more of their original stake). Ben says about $223B and David about $230B. Ken earned his 5% for raising the money, and he also invested about $100K.

LessonAisle 04
04

Control can be worth more than the check

The Cadillac was a symptom. The real question was whose company it would be. Walking away cost nothing, and scarcity raised the price. In Ken’s business, unsold goods get marked up.

05Aisle
five
1978

Pat

The fourth founder showed up an hour late to his own store, wearing a powder-blue velvet leisure suit and gold chains.

P
Pat FarrahMerchant behind HomeCo in Los Angeles, a 130,000 sq ft hardware warehouse stacked to the ceiling. In Ken’s telling, crazy but a genius.

Bernie and Arthur found their concept already running in LA. HomeCo was a hardware Price Club, with merchandise piled to the rafters and customers buying in a frenzy. The philosophy was to stack it high and watch it fly. Pat Farrah ran it. Legend says he once drove a forklift through a wall that the inspectors hadn’t approved.

The team signed a letter of intent to buy HomeCo with their $2 million. Due diligence found that the sales were real but the store was insolvent. Pat hadn’t been paying suppliers. Invoices due in 30, 60 and 90 days were piling up. He wasn’t dishonest. He just didn’t know how to run the business side, and his margins were far thinner than he thought.

So they didn’t buy HomeCo. Pat let it go bankrupt and joined them as the fourth co-founder, running merchandising. He later gave HomeCo’s investors shares to make them whole. In four words, Ben’s summary: Pat needed an Arthur.

The lesson for a company with only $2 million was all about working capital. Get the longest supplier terms possible. Turn inventory quickly so customers pay before the supplier bill comes due. Avoid offering credit early on, which in those years meant favoring cash-paying DIY customers over contractors who expected to run a tab. Ben notes that even today, about half of Home Depot’s inventory is effectively financed by its suppliers.

Interactive · model it

Who pays for the shelves?

Goods sit on the shelf for 365 ÷ turns days. Suppliers wait payment terms days for their money. Whatever share of that shelf time the terms cover is inventory the supplier is financing.

LessonAisle 05
05

Genius needs a counterweight, and cash comes from working capital

Pat brought the merchandising magic and Arthur brought the discipline. Supplier terms, fast turns and no credit are how $2 million could fund a chain.

06Aisle
six
June 22, 1979 · Atlanta

Opening Day

Low ceilings, linoleum floors, borrowed boxes and two thousand empty paint cans.

Why Atlanta? The Southeast was growing fast, real estate was cheap, and J.C. Penney was shutting down Treasure Island, its Kmart copycat. Penney sublet them four empty boxes in the suburbs. A marketing consultant pitched the name “Bad Bernie’s Build-All,” with Bernie in jail for charging prices too low. They went with an investor’s wife’s suggestion instead: The Home Depot. The initials matched Handy Dan’s. The consultant did get the color right. Orange stood out, and cheap circus-tent canvas made the signs and the aprons.

The first two stores opened the same day, June 22, 1979, and nearly every planned detail went wrong. The newspaper ad didn’t run, so staff stood in the parking lots handing out dollar bills to lure people inside. Store managers had polished the floors overnight as a surprise. Pat arrived around 4 a.m., saw the shine, and woke Bernie and Arthur. They drove forklifts around to scuff the floors and sprinkled sawdust so the stores looked busy.

With only $2 million, they couldn’t stock 25,000 products to the ceiling, so they faked the abundance. Tap the cards below to see how.

Interactive · tap each card

What customers saw, and what was there

The model worked anyway. Prices were 10–25% below competitors, gross margin was about 30%, and goods came on pallets straight from manufacturers. A third Atlanta store opened by the end of 1979. That year lost about $1 million of the $2 million. In 1980 the company made about $1 million. The playbook was to saturate one metro, become No. 1 there, then move on, so the ad budget covered several stores at once. Bernie’s line was that their stores were places of action.

LessonAisle 06
06

A store is a stage, and abundance is a feeling

Customers trusted the low prices partly because the store felt like a busy warehouse. The founders built that feeling before they could afford the inventory.

07Aisle
seven
The 1980s

The Operating System

Anyone could copy the big orange box. The system inside it was much harder to copy.

Retail usually trades off price, selection and convenience. Home Depot chose the first two and gave up the third. You drove out to a cheap lot in the sticks, but you only made one trip. Bernie had a hunch that returns rose with size. In 1980 the stores were about twice the size of a Lowe’s and carried about three times the products, but they rang up about four times the transactions.

1980 · Home Depot store vs. Lowe’s store

Bernie’s hunch

Ratios as cited by Ben from Arvind Navaratnam’s research (Worldly Partners). Transactions grew faster than space, so the store got more productive as it got bigger.

Copycats arrived with names like Builders Square, Home Club, HQ and Mr. How. They built the warehouse but not the system. Its key piece was the people. Home Depot hired plumbers, electricians and carpenters to work the floor. For a tradesperson, that meant steady hours, no driving between jobs, less wear on the body, and often their first retirement plan. For customers it meant real advice, the one thing Costco and Walmart can’t easily add. Nobody needs expert help to buy $10,000 of paper towels.

Company lore has a story about a faucet. A customer came in to replace a leaky one. An associate sold him a 25-cent washer instead of a $200 faucet. The customer came back and spent about $100,000 remodeling his kitchen. A critic said the associate had cost the company a sale. Bernie promoted him.

Ownership went all the way down. Salaried staff from assistant store manager up got stock options. Hourly associates could buy shares at a 15% discount, and the company guaranteed them against losses below their purchase price. Training connected work on the floor to the stock price, and many early associates became millionaires. Headquarters was called the Store Support Center, and the org chart was drawn upside down, with customers on top and the CEO at the bottom.

Model: product cost is fixed at 55% of the old price, so a 21% price cut brings gross margin from 45% to about 30%, which matches the founders’ plan. Revenue figures come from the pitch ($3M for the best Handy Dan, $7–9M planned).

LessonAisle 07
07

Margin dollars pay the bills, not margin percent

The new store had a thinner margin and fatter profits. Low prices brought more trips, more volume, better supplier terms and lower costs, and the savings went back into prices and people.

LessonAisle 07
08

Expertise is the moat, and equity keeps it there

Hiring tradespeople made 25,000 products easy to navigate, and general merchants couldn’t copy that. Giving every associate ownership made the 25-cent washer the rational choice.

08Aisle
eight
1981 – 1999

Going National

An IPO with interest rates near 20%, a $32 million valuation, and a new store every four days.

J.C. Penney called again, this time with Florida leases. The company needed cash to take them. In 1981 interest rates were at or near 20%. Ken was now a principal investor and couldn’t underwrite the deal himself, so friends at Bear Stearns took it as a favor. The plan was to raise $6 million, half for expansion and half to let seed investors cash out at about twice their money. The week before pricing, Bear cut the deal roughly in half. Ken told the seed investors not to sell. The IPO raised about $4 million in all, at a $32 million market cap after the offering.

Then the company spread. First Florida, then Texas, where buying a copycat chain called Bowater turned into a costly rebuild. Next came California, the home of Handy Dan, then the Northeast and then the rest of the country. Home Depot sold suppliers and lenders on a future it hadn’t built yet, with promises like 50 stores down the road, and then built it. In 1989 it passed Lowe’s to become the largest home improvement retailer in the U.S. That same year, Handy Dan went out of business.

Interactive · hover the points

Forty-seven years in one chart

Shaded by CEO era. Store counts are the episode’s figures where given (1984, 1986, 1989, 1996, 2000, 2008, today), with company-reported counts filling gaps. Revenue is by fiscal year from annual reports. FY2006 includes HD Supply, which was sold in 2007. All figures are approximate.

The 1990s added the Pro. Home Depot built a Pro desk, business credit accounts, contractor-grade brands like DeWalt and Milwaukee, volume pricing and job-site delivery. By 1996 sales were about $20 billion, a new store opened roughly every four days, and Home Depot was a top sponsor of the Atlanta Olympics alongside Coca-Cola, Visa and Nike. About 75% of store managers had no college degree. They had been promoted from the floor.

There were cracks. In 1997 Bernie handed the CEO job to Arthur. That same year the company settled one of the largest gender-discrimination suits of its time, though the founders dispute the claims in their book. Decentralization, a source of strength, had gone too far: Bernie credited local buying with 15–20% higher sales per store, but at one point 57 different buyers were negotiating with the same suppliers. And Lowe’s had changed. In 1990 it gave up its small stores, built warehouses, and aimed them at the shoppers Home Depot ignored: casual DIYers, women, and people sprucing up for the weekend. Its slogan, “Improving Home Improvement,” was aimed squarely at Home Depot.

LessonAisle 08
09

Sell the future, then make it come true

Ben’s point: promising suppliers and lenders 50 stores you don’t have is fine as long as you actually build them. Home Depot spent the 1980s turning those promises into stores.

09Aisle
nine
2000 – January 2, 2007

The GE Man

Revenue doubled, the stock went nowhere, and the board skipped its own shareholder meeting.

By 2000, Home Depot had more than $40 billion in revenue, more than 1,000 stores and more than 200,000 employees. It had no internal successor. The board spent six months courting Jamie Dimon, who had just been pushed out of Citigroup. Then GE’s succession race ended. In November 2000, Jack Welch chose Jeff Immelt. The two losing finalists were Jim McNerney, who went to 3M, and Bob Nardelli.

Ken sat on GE’s board, too. He called Nardelli and used the same golden-horseshoe line he had once used on Bernie. The offer was president and COO, with a path to CEO and about $150 million in equity to make up for his GE options. Nardelli then insisted on being CEO immediately. Arthur said yes, though he didn’t mean it, and was gone within about six months.

Nardelli said the company had been in startup mode for 20 years, and he brought GE’s playbook. He merged nine buying offices into one, which won better supplier terms. He installed Six Sigma and new systems. Ken still says everything Nardelli touched in his first four years turned to gold. But Nardelli also swapped experienced floor staff for part-timers, and he preferred college graduates for store manager jobs, which closed off the path from the floor.

2000 → 2006

Two scoreboards

On the spreadsheet
  • ▲Revenue roughly doubled
  • ▲Stores ~1,100 → ~2,000
  • ▲Gross margin ~30% → ~33%
  • ▲~$20B returned in buybacks and dividends
  • ▲HD Supply built to 13% of revenue
On the store floor
  • ▼Associates per store ~200 → ~170
  • ▼Customer satisfaction: from near the top to last among major retailers
  • ▼Path from apron to store manager narrowed
  • ▼Stock −12% over five years; Lowe’s +173%
  • ▼CEO pay ~$200M over six years

Staffing from Arvind Navaratnam’s research. The stock comparison is from Joe Nocera’s May 2006 New York Times column. The other figures are as stated by the hosts.

The higher margin was the quiet problem. Home Depot had won by passing its scale savings back to customers. Now it was keeping them. Meanwhile the housing boom hid the damage, and Lowe’s took the weekend shoppers. Nardelli also refused to tie his pay to the stock price. That was defensible in theory but jarring at a company built on employee ownership.

The 2006 annual meeting in Wilmington, Del., became the symbol. No directors showed up. Nardelli ran the meeting alone, and a shareholder’s microphone was cut off. On January 2, 2007, Ken called a special board meeting in Dallas, and Nardelli was out. He left with $18 million in cash severance and a retirement package the hosts put at about $210 million. Associates were reportedly high-fiving in the stores. Nardelli went on to run Chrysler.

B

Pushed hard enough, operational excellence can squeeze the entrepreneurship out of a company. Six Sigma treats the person in the aisle as a replaceable part. Home Depot’s whole model depended on that person.

Ben’s argument, paraphrased
LessonAisle 09
10

You can optimize away the thing that makes you work

Every metric Nardelli moved was real, but the thing he cut, the knowledgeable associate, was the moat. Operations and service pulled in opposite directions, and service lost.

10Aisle
ten
2007 – 2014

The Turnaround

The new CEO was another GE man. His first call was to Bernie.

F
Frank BlakeA former lawyer, Supreme Court clerk, federal official and GE M&A chief who came over with Nardelli. He had never run a P&L. His son worked in a Home Depot store.

Bernie was furious that the board had picked yet another GE man. On January 2, 2007, Frank Blake’s first act as CEO was to call him. Then Blake and Ken flew to Florida for breakfast, and Blake and Bernie walked a store together. They started at a Costco, not a Home Depot.

Blake brought the inverted pyramid back. He asked to take 90% of his pay in stock options, which Ben calls one way to make a statement. And he had a different way of judging culture. Silicon Valley tends to see employees watching the share price as a distraction. Blake saw associates checking the stock price in the break room as a sign of a healthy culture.

He also took over just as housing collapsed. Revenue fell from 2007, bottomed in 2010, and didn’t get back to its 2007 level until 2014.

Blake made three capital decisions that the hosts think define the era.

He stopped building stores. In 2008 there were about 2,300. Blake closed around 30, wrote off about $1 billion of the planned pipeline, and then opened only four or five a year for roughly a decade. Sales per store went from about $30 million to about $65 million. Ben’s view is that opening stores had been a crutch. As long as the store count kept growing, nobody had to make the existing stores better.

He sold HD Supply to private equity in 2007 for about $8.3 billion, and he bought back stock with the proceeds, about 14% of the shares in the first year. Over his tenure the share count fell about 30%, mostly at $30–50 a share. At recording, the stock was around $340.

He rebuilt the supply chain. Starting in 2009, suppliers shipped to new rapid deployment centers instead of straight to each store, and the RDCs sent mixed loads on to the stores. That backbone later handled e-commerce. The hosts say this is where Ken atoned for the Nardelli years.

Each square ≈ 1% of shares when Blake took over

The quiet compounding of buybacks

~30%of shares retired
~8×$40 then vs ~$340 now

Shares retired over Blake’s tenure, about 30% per the episode, at a rough midpoint price of $40. Each remaining share now owns about 1.4 times as much of the company.

LessonAisle 10
11

More stores aren’t automatically better

Ben’s point: opening stores isn’t a virtue on its own. Make each store more productive, put the cash into the network, and buy back your own stock when it’s cheap.

11Aisle
eleven
2009 – 2021

Heavy, Urgent, Local

Why Amazon never ate the hardware store.

In the hosts’ telling, the first real internet threat wasn’t Amazon. It was YouTube. Around 2006 and 2007, the know-how that once lived in the aisles moved online. But the products themselves didn’t fit Amazon well.

Lumber, drywall, roofing and insulation are heavy and bulky. David’s deck example: about 200 cubic feet and 6,000 pounds of lumber, roughly the weight of two midsize cars. The work is also urgent. The customer is usually halfway through a project, and if they run out of nails, the whole job stops. Ben tested it. A ship-from-store order reached his house from the Seattle SoDo store in about two hours, while an online-only item took about two and a half days.

One dot = one facility

The network behind the stores

~2,400stores, double as mini-warehouses
2–24 hdelivery target for 90% of U.S. homes

Counts as listed in the episode. Today’s promise, per David, is more than a million products to a home, job site or nearby store within 2 to 24 hours.

When COVID arrived, Home Depot had spent a decade not building stores and instead building distribution and buy-online, pick-up-in-store. The hosts call it the most incredible unintentional preparation of all time. Revenue went from about $110 billion to the $150–160 billion range almost overnight.

LessonAisle 11
12

Heavy, urgent and local beats e-commerce

When the product weighs a ton, the customer needs it today, and a store sits within a few miles, the store is the warehouse. Logistics became the core skill.

12Aisle
twelve
2014 – today

The Pro

Half the business is now people who do this for a living.

Blake retired in 2014 and, unlike his predecessors, left a bench. Craig Menear ran the company for about eight years, and Ted Decker took over in 2022. Alumni spread across corporate America: Carol Tomé went on to run UPS, Tom Taylor runs Floor & Decor, and Marvin Ellison, who ran stores under Blake, has been CEO of Lowe’s since 2018.

The strategy is the Pro. Roughly half of sales go to contractors, remodelers and property managers, and they look nothing like weekend customers.

A year of visits, one tick per trip

Weekend warrior vs. Pro

13×more trips
20×more spend

2015 averages cited by Ben: DIY customers about 5 visits and $330 a year, Pros about 66 visits and $6,500. Visit dates are scattered randomly for illustration.

To reach Pros beyond the store, Home Depot spent big. In 2020 it bought back the most valuable part of HD Supply for about $8 billion. Then, in 2024, it made the largest deal in its history: SRS Distribution, for about $18.25 billion. SRS serves roofers, landscapers and pool contractors with planned bulk orders and its own delivery fleet. Buybacks were paused to pay for it. A later multibillion-dollar deal took SRS into drywall and ceilings.

The hosts point out that this is Nardelli’s strategy, adjacencies through supply businesses. His idea was right, they argue. His timing and method were wrong. Back then the core business was weakening. Now logistics is the core competency, so the adjacencies fit.

Home Depot, by the numbers

The analysis

Checkout

After the story, the hosts step back to ask what made Home Depot special, where its advantages come from, and why it got so big.

Analysis I

The Paradox of Specialness

Ben’s thesis is that what makes a company special early often holds it back at scale. Home Depot has dropped almost every tactic from its early days. Use the switch to compare.

Interactive

Then and now

There are two ways to read this. One is entropy: companies get less special as they grow, and only a few, such as Costco, Hermès and Vanguard, resist it. The other is that dropping early tactics is usually right. David notes that markets change. The 1979 company didn’t need fulfillment centers, and today’s company would be finished without them.

LessonAnalysis
13

Keep the founding values, not the founding tactics

Ben argues that the values matter and the tactics probably don’t. Hermès hand-stitching is the rare tactic that is the value. Most are just scaffolding.

Analysis II

Seven Powers

Using Hamilton Helmer’s framework, the hosts find one big power and a few smaller ones. Scale is the big one. Home Depot is about three times the size of Lowe’s and gets the best supplier prices and private-label manufacturers. But they also note that Home Depot is only a little more profitable than Lowe’s, and the gap is shrinking.

The meters show how strongly the hosts lean on each power. Network economies, cornered resource and process power weren’t argued for in the episode.

Analysis III

Why it got so big

Ben’s closing framework treats Home Depot’s size as a product of several factors, not a sum. In a product, if any one factor is zero, the whole thing is zero. Turn off a factor to see what happens.

$350B

David adds one more factor: American policy. Mortgage subsidies, tax breaks and a culture of owning your home all feed the market. China has a bigger housing market but almost no home improvement market. The wealthy there live in city apartments and don’t do their own repairs, and Home Depot’s China venture failed.

Coda

The value is in the holding

Ken Langone, about to turn 91, has never sold a share. His stake is worth about $6 billion. Holding it meant sitting through a drop of about two-thirds in 1985 and drops of about 70% in 2002 and 2008. That original 5% stake compounded at about 25% a year for nearly half a century. Ben’s takeaway is that the returns came from holding on.

The value is in the holding

The 25% compounding was only available to people who held through three crashes of two-thirds or more. Buying was the easy part.

Sources & credits

The episode. Acquired, “The Home Depot” (Fall 2026, Episode 2), hosted by Ben Gilbert and David Rosenthal. This page is an unofficial companion. Except for one quoted line from Ken Langone, everything here is paraphrased. Figures are the hosts’ unless marked. Where Ben and David gave different numbers, both are noted.

The hosts’ sources include Built from Scratch by Bernie Marcus and Arthur Blank, Ken Langone’s I Love Capitalism!, Bernie’s memoir Kick Up Some Dust, Arvind Navaratnam’s research for Worldly Partners, and an interview with Frank Blake.

Revenue history in the growth chart comes from Home Depot annual reports (fiscal years). Filler store counts are company-reported and approximate.

Illustrations. Every painting is a watercolor rendering made with OpenCV from a freely licensed photograph on Wikimedia Commons. Each caption names the photographer and license. Adaptations of CC BY-SA images are shared under the same license. The portrait blots and brush washes are procedurally generated.
